rules.title: Gift-card or voucher payment request
rules.why: Gift cards are irreversible and untraceable, which is why they are the favourite currency of CEO-fraud and sextortion scams. No real business requests payment in gift cards.
rules.advice: Stop. Never buy gift cards on instruction from an email. Call the requester on a number you already know.
negations: we never ask for gift cards
examples: I need you to buy two $100 Amazon gift cards urgently and send me the codes.
falsePositives: Marketing mail advertising gift cards; the rule keys on a request to buy and send codes.

rules.title: Change of bank account or payment details
rules.why: Swapping the payee account on an invoice is the core of payment-diversion fraud. Once the money moves to the attacker's account it is usually unrecoverable.
rules.advice: Verify any change of bank details by phoning a known contact at the supplier. Never accept new account details from email alone.

values: make payment to the new account

examples: Please note our new bank details below and update your records before the next payment.
falsePositives: Legitimate suppliers do change banks, but always verify by phone; that is exactly why this stays a strong signal.

rules.title: Urgent payment or transfer demand
rules.why: Pressure to send money quickly via wire, UPI or crypto is designed to beat any verification process.
rules.advice: Verify the request independently before sending any money, especially if it is urgent.
examples: Please process the urgent payment today to avoid disruption.
falsePositives: Genuine invoices and payment reminders; consider sender authentication and whether YOU expected the bill.

rules.title: Cryptocurrency wallet address in a payment context
rules.why: A wallet address plus payment wording is a strong sign of ransomware, sextortion or investment fraud. The address itself is only meaningful with that context, which is why the rule demands a nearby payment term.
rules.advice: Never send crypto to an address from an email. Crypto payments cannot be reversed.
examples: Send 0.5 BTC to bc1qexampleaddress to restore your files.
falsePositives: A developer sharing an address in a technical discussion; weak alone, hence weight 15.

rules.title: Unexpected invoice, purchase order or overdue notice
rules.why: Fake invoices and remittance notices are used both to trigger payment and to deliver malware as an 'invoice' attachment. They work because they look routine.
rules.advice: Check the invoice against orders you actually placed. Never open an invoice attachment you did not expect.
examples: Please find attached invoice INV-88213 overdue for payment.
falsePositives: Regular vendor invoices are legitimate; the unexpected ones are the risk, which the tool cannot know - it flags the pattern.

rules.title: Callback request involving a phone number and a refund or charge
rules.why: Callback phishing (TOAD) hides the fraud behind a phone number instead of a link, because phone calls bypass email link scanners. The victim is talked into installing remote-access software.
rules.advice: Do not call numbers from an email. Look up the company's number yourself and call that. Never install remote-access tools on request.
examples: Your subscription renewed for $499. To cancel, call our helpline on +1-800-555-0199.
falsePositives: Support signatures legitimately include phone numbers; weight rises only with a refund/charge/cancel context.
